summary: For ages 7-9, this topic uses the wow-factor of record-breaking insects (dung beetle strength, flea jumps, dragonfly speed, bombardier beetle spray) to teach the core cognitive move: comparing feats RELATIVE to body size, not in absolute units. Learners name record-breakers, scale a feat to the human body (flea jump = clearing a skyscraper), and explain WHY being tiny and light enables huge feats per body-length. The discriminating understanding is separating 'strongest/fastest for its size' from 'strongest/fastest overall', and grasping that scaling an insect up would not preserve the feat because weight grows faster than strength.
misconceptions: 'These feats are big in absolute terms' — they're extreme RELATIVE to tiny body size, not in metres/kilograms.
'Bigger animals are always stronger' — strength-to-weight favours the very small.
'It's just random trivia' — the feats follow from body structure and size.
'Insects are weak because they're small' — smallness is precisely what enables the records.
Confusing fastest/strongest/highest-jumping as if one insect holds every record.

activities.title: Insect Hall of Records: reveal the feat, then scale it to you
steps: Meet four record-breakers and their feats: one kind of dung beetle (the horned dung beetle, which can pull more than a thousand times its own body weight), the flea (jumps over 150 times its body length), the dragonfly (among the fastest-flying insects), and the bombardier beetle (sprays a hot, noxious chemical).

For each champion, first state the raw feat, then convert it to human scale: e.g. 'a flea's jump is like a person leaping over a skyscraper'; 'the dung beetle's pull is like a grown-up dragging about six double-decker buses (or you, a lighter child, dragging about two)'.
For each feat, answer a 'why can it do this?' prompt that links the feat to body structure: small size, light body, exoskeleton, and muscle/leverage.
Sort the champions by which record each holds (strongest for its size, a top jumper for its size, one of the fastest fliers) so no single insect is mistakenly credited with every record.
activities.insight: Numbers alone ('150 times', 'hundreds of times') mean little until mapped onto the child's own body; the human-scale comparison is what makes the feat astonishing, and the feat follows from body structure and size rather than being random trivia.

activities.title: Scale it yourself: slider and strength tester
steps: Use a scale control that maps an insect feat onto a human in real time — slide a flea's jump multiplier and watch a person-figure leap higher and higher relative to known buildings.
Use a 'can it lift this?' strength tester: stack weights on a dung beetle and compare to stacking the equivalent ratio onto a human figure.
State in your own words what the slider shows: the feat is enormous measured in body-lengths or body-weights, even though in plain metres or kilograms a human moves or jumps far more in total.
activities.insight: Manipulating the comparison is intended to make the relative-to-size idea something felt, not just read: the ratio is huge while the absolute amount is modest, and these are two different claims.

activities.title: Would a giant flea still win? Reasoning about scaling
steps: Discuss the diagnostic question: a flea jumps about 150 times its body length, but a person cannot jump anywhere near 150 times their height — does that mean a flea has stronger muscles than a person? Explain what is really going on.
Argue whether a flea blown up to human size would still jump 150 times its body length, and why.
Give an example that separates 'strongest for its size' from 'strongest of all' — e.g. who could actually move a heavy brick, the person or the insect?
activities.insight: The record is a ratio, not a total; being small and light is the reason the feat is huge per body-length. Scaled up, the body would weigh far more (weight grows faster than strength), so the feat could not be repeated — the feat depends on being tiny.

activities.title: Brag battle: record-holders in role (optional extension)
steps: In role, voice a record-holder insect boasting about its feat, then have it correctly qualify the boast: 'I'm the strongest — for my size.'
Challenge another champion so the group clarifies which record belongs to which insect.
Use the in-role talk to practise explaining WHY the feat works (small, light, exoskeleton leverage), not just that it exists.
activities.insight: Putting the qualification 'for its size' into the insect's own boast is intended to reinforce the relative-versus-absolute distinction in a memorable, playful way.

checkQuestion: A flea can jump about 150 times its own body length. A grown-up person can jump nowhere near 150 times their own height. Does that mean a flea has stronger muscles than a person? Explain what's really going on — why can such a tiny creature do such an enormous jump for its size?
checkAnswer: No, it doesn't mean the flea has stronger muscles than a whole person — a person's muscles are far more powerful in total. What's really going on is that being very SMALL and light makes extreme feats possible RELATIVE to body size: a tiny body weighs very little, so its muscles (and springy body parts) can fling it a huge distance compared to its own length. Measured against its own size the flea wins, but that's because it's small and light, not because a flea is stronger than a human overall.
